extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, natural-rights theory, and legal/political history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting John Locke's normative principles about parental power, individual freedom, conjugal society, and the origins/limits of political authority from Two Treatises (Chapters on parental and civil society).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural equality in respect of jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: All men by nature are equal in respect of jurisdiction or dominion one over another; every man hath an equal right to his natural freedom, without being subjected to the will or authority of any other man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes sorts of equality (age, virtue, merit, birth may create precedence) but insists the natural equality relevant to political power is equality of jurisdiction — no natural dominion of one man over another. This equality is the baseline for arguments against paternal/monarchical absolute rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children born to freedom but temporarily subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Children are born to freedom but not born in the full exercise of it; parents have a temporary rule and jurisdiction over them during infancy and minority until age and reason loosen those bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental authority is likened to swaddling-clothes: necessary supports during weakness. As children grow, age and reason remove parental control; when a child attains the use of reason he is presumed capable of self-government and thus free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law’s purpose: to preserve and enlarge freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of law is not to abolish or restrain but to preserve and enlarge freedom; where there is no law there is no freedom, and freedom is not a licence to do anything but a liberty to order one's person and possessions within the bounds of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains 'law' as direction for free and intelligent agents toward the general good; this legitimates temporary parental direction as protective rather than oppressive. Laws (natural or civil) define liberties — true freedom exists under law, not in lawlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power grounded in duty to preserve, nourish, and educate
rubrics_metrics.description: The power parents have over children arises from the duty incumbent on them to preserve, nourish and educate offspring during their imperfect childhood; parents must inform the mind and govern actions of the nonage until reason takes its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grounding in parental duty distinguishes parental authority from ownership or sovereign dominion: it is functional and fiduciary — directed to the child's good and to preparing the child for freedom, not to perpetual rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental authority terminates with the child’s maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: The bonds of subjection are temporary and terminate when the child attains sufficient age and reason to know the law and dispose of his own actions; thereafter the father has no dominion over the life, liberty, or estate of his son beyond that of any other man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke ties legal capacity (e.g., English law presuming capacity at 21) to freedom. Parental government ends with nonage; duties of honour remain but not coercive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those incapable of reason remain under guardianship
rubrics_metrics.description: If through defects any one never attains the use of reason (lunatics, idiots), they are never capable of being free men and are continued under the tuition and government of others as long as their understanding is uncapable of that charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats incapacity as a durable exception: permanent guardianship is justified by continued inability to be guided by reason; guardians are to seek and procure the good of those under them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power is not absolute nor regal and is shared with the mother
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental power scarcely amounts to an instance of regal authority; it is not absolute, and by nature belongs to both parents — mothers share the power and rights regarding care, discipline and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke criticizes arguments that equate fatherhood with monarchy: if parental power were truly absolute, mothers would share it equally; the temporary and care-based nature of parental power undercuts claims of inherent monarchical authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power has defined limits (no legislative or capital punishment authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The father's power is limited to discipline and education necessary for children's wellbeing and does not extend to making standing laws, enforcing penalties reaching estate, liberty, limbs or life, nor to permanent legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke insists the father cannot, by virtue of being a parent, exact capital punishments or create perpetual binding laws over his children — such powers properly belong to magistrates, not parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filial honour is lifelong and distinct from obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the temporary subjection during minority, children owe a perpetual obligation of honour, respect, gratitude, support, defence and assistance to their parents that continues all their life, but this is distinct from absolute obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that honour involves inward esteem and outward expressions and can require defence and support, yet it does not grant parents coercive legislative power over adult children. Degrees of obligation may vary with parents' care and kindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental authority attaches to the duty of care and can be delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of tuition belongs to whoever has the care, nourishment and education of the child; if the father quits his care or places the child under others (apprenticeship, foster parents, tutors), the authority goes with that care and is alienable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses examples (apprenticeship, foster parents) to show parental authority is functional and transferible; the mere act of begetting confers little if no ongoing care accompanies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance and property can be used as ties to obedience but submission is voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Fathers commonly have influence by bestowing estates; possession of the father's land is the expectation of children and can be bestowed more or less liberally, creating a tie on obedience — but political submission annexed to land is voluntary by those who accept the inheritance on its conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes between natural ties and voluntary conditions attached to property; heirs who take land accept the political conditions inherent in that possession, rather than being naturally bound by paternal compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power is distinct from paternal power and originates in consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Political (civil) power is perfectly distinct from paternal power, built on different foundations and given to different ends; political authority arose by the consent of people, not by any natural paternal right, though household rule could evolve into public rule by tacit consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that early family heads became rulers largely by tacit or convenient consent; this historical development does not establish a natural paternal basis for political sovereignty. Consent, not lineage, grounds legitimate political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal society is a voluntary compact for procreation and mutual support
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugal society (marriage) is a voluntary compact between man and woman, primarily for procreation and the continuation of the species, drawing with it mutual support, assistance, and communion of interests necessary for their offspring's nourishment and maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke compares human mating to animals: human conjugal bonds last longer because human offspring require prolonged joint care. The compact’s duration and terms can be determined by consent unless positive law ordains permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority within marriage is limited and tied to ends; husband’s rule is not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Where differences of will arise within conjugal society, it naturally falls to the man to have the last determination (as the abler and stronger) for common interests, but this reaches only common concerns and property; the wife retains full possession of her peculiar rights and the husband has no absolute power over her life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke cautions that conjugal rule is functional, not sovereign: community of goods, maintenance and mutual assistance may be regulated by contract; civil magistrate intervenes only to decide controversies, not to abridge rights essential to marriage’s ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age/discretion determines capacity for civic acts (oaths, allegiance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonwealths recognise a time when men begin to act like free men; until that time they do not require oaths of fealty, allegiance or other public owning of the government — capacity to know the law (age of discretion) makes one fit for civic duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke ties civic capacities to the same standard as parental termination of rule: maturity of reason and understanding. The law presumes an age (e.g., twenty-one) at which individuals can be held to civic obligations.
